issues.body:
Um contentor **privilegiado** recebe `/proc/sys` montado só de leitura. O `kube-proxy` do kubeadm falha por isso, e com ele fica todo o plano de serviço do cluster: sem `kube-proxy` não há ClusterIP, e o `coredns` fica preso em `ContainerCreating` à espera dele.

## O erro, textual

```
I sysctls.go:147 "Setting nf_conntrack_max" nfConntrackMax=131072
E server.go:136  "Error running ProxyServer" err="could not set conntrack parameters
                 from kube-proxy configuration: open /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max:
                 read-only file system"
running command: exit status 1
```

## O que está medido

| | |
|---|---|
| o `kube-proxy` pede privilégio | `kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-proxy -o jsonpath='{…securityContext}'` → `{"privileged":true}` |
| o ficheiro existe no host | `/proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max` — presente, escrevível |
| dentro do contentor | `read-only file system` |
| efeito | `kube-proxy` em `CrashLoopBackOff` nos dois nós; `coredns` em `ContainerCreating` |

## Comportamento esperado

Pela OCI runtime spec, e pelo que o containerd e o CRI-O fazem, um contentor com `privileged: true` recebe `/proc/sys` **escrevível** — sem `maskedPaths` nem `readonlyPaths`. É precisamente por isso que o `kube-proxy` pode existir como carga de Kubernetes em vez de um daemon do host.

## O que NÃO é

Vale a pena dizer, porque persegui as duas hipóteses erradas antes desta:

- **Não é** o kubelet a matar os pods. Medido: `computePodActions` dá `KillPod: false` para o `etcd` (×20) e para o `kube-apiserver` (×17). Os `KillPod: true` que aparecem no jornal são quase todos do `coredns`, que é vítima e não causa.
- **Não é** o `PodSandboxStatus` do #233. Esse está corrigido e nota-se: os quatro static pods do control-plane sobrevivem, o cluster converge, e os dois nós ficam `Ready`.

## Estado do cluster com este defeito presente

```
delonix-stage-cp1   Ready   control-plane   81m   v1.36.4
delonix-stage-w1    Ready   <none>          76m   v1.36.4

etcd / kube-apiserver / kube-controller-manager / kube-scheduler   Running
kube-proxy                                                        CrashLoopBackOff
coredns                                                           ContainerCreating
```

Ou seja: o control-plane inteiro funciona. **Este é o único componente partido**, e é o que separa um cluster que arranca de um cluster que serve.

## Como reproduzir

```bash
delonix cluster kubeadm --name t --network <rede> --control-plane 1 --workers 1 \
  --vm-image delonix-vm-k8s:1.36 --k8s-version 1.36.4
# depois, no nó:
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-proxy | grep conntrack
```

Ou, mais directo, sem Kubernetes pelo meio:

```bash
delonix container run --privileged --rm alpine \
  sh -c 'echo 131072 > /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max'
```

## Não validado

Não li o código que monta o `/proc` no `delonix-cri`, nem confirmei se o mesmo acontece pelo caminho do `delonix container run --privileged` fora do CRI — a segunda reprodução acima é uma hipótese por confirmar, não uma medição. O que está medido é o caminho do CRI, com o `kube-proxy` real.

Medido a 2026-09-07 contra a golden `delonix-vm-k8s:1.36-motor2` (`delonix 2.0.0`, commit `4eaf44355`), Kubernetes 1.36.4, backend libvirt.

comments.body:
**Correcção ao corpo desta issue.** Escrevi lá:

> «o control-plane inteiro funciona. **Este é o único componente partido**»

**É falso.** Li um instante e chamei-lhe estado. Medido depois, ao longo do tempo:

```
reinícios totais:  125 → 126 em 75 segundos

etcd                       20 reinícios
kube-apiserver             20
kube-controller-manager    19   CrashLoopBackOff
kube-scheduler             21   CrashLoopBackOff
```

E numa observação de quatro minutos, amostrada de minuto a minuto, o apiserver esteve **indisponível nas quatro amostras**.

O que continua verdadeiro, e é o âmbito desta issue: o `kube-proxy` falha por `/proc/sys` só de leitura num contentor privilegiado. Isso é determinístico, literal, e independente do resto.

O ciclo de reinícios do control-plane é **outro defeito**, com outra cadeia, e não depende deste — o `etcd` não precisa de `kube-proxy` para funcionar. Fica em issue própria para não misturar dois problemas num sítio só.

Nota de método, porque custou três conclusões erradas nesta investigação: `kubectl get nodes` dizia `Ready` nos dois nós enquanto o control-plane reiniciava vinte vezes. A coluna que conta é a de reinícios, e a amostra tem de ser repetida.

**Resolvido e provado contra um cluster real** — correcção no [#239](https://github.com/angolardevops/delonix-runtime/pull/239).

```
CRI no nó:   12 882 328 bytes   ← binário com a correcção
kube-proxy:  sem erro de read-only no log
cluster:     rc=0
```

A causa final não era só a que esta issue descreve. Os `--masked-path`/`--readonly-path` explícitos eram **metade** do problema: retirá-los faz o motor cair nas omissões do runc, que também contêm `/proc/sys`. O que faltava era o CRI **passar `--privileged` ao motor** — traduzia `privileged: true` em `--cap-add ALL` e parava aí.

Capacidades e montagens são eixos separados do `--privileged`. A nota do `cap_ceiling` já o dizia; o código fazia metade.

Fica aberto o [#238](https://github.com/angolardevops/delonix-runtime/issues/238), que é independente: neste mesmo cluster, com o `kube-proxy` a funcionar, o apiserver continua a cair.

**Reaberta: a correcção do #239 não resolve isto, e a minha validação estava errada.**

Medido no cluster `prova239`, construído com a golden que leva o binário corrigido:

```
open /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max: read-only file system
kube-proxy   Error   r=41 / r=33     (log 42 do contentor)
coredns      Pending
```

O erro é o mesmo, no cluster que devia prová-lo resolvido.

**Onde falhei:** o meu script de validação procurava `read-only file system` no log *mais recente* num instante único — e nesse momento o contentor tinha acabado de arrancar e ainda não tinha escrito a linha. Li «não encontrei» como «não acontece». Com base nisso afirmei que estava provado, o #239 foi fundido e esta issue fechada.

**O que falta distinguir**, e são duas medições simples:

1. o `--privileged` não chega ao contentor — vê-se no comando com que o CRI o arrancou;
2. chega e o motor não o honra neste caminho — vê-se com `delonix container run --privileged … sh -c 'echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max'`.

Não fiz nenhuma das duas. O #239 fica na `main` como está; não proponho recuá-lo sem saber qual das duas é.

Corrigido na main: #318 (a038c87b) devolve `/proc/sys` gravável a um container privileged, e #322 fecha o resto do caminho do nó root. Reconfirmado em 2026-09-19 no HEAD 85c19674: `--privileged` escreve `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward`; um container normal continua com `/proc/sys` em ro.

issues.body:
O control-plane de um cluster `delonix cluster kubeadm` reinicia em ciclo. Os nós dizem `Ready`, e mesmo assim o `etcd` e o `kube-apiserver` vão em vinte reinícios cada, com o `scheduler` e o `controller-manager` em `CrashLoopBackOff` atrás deles.

Não é o `#237` — o `etcd` não precisa do `kube-proxy`.

## A cadeia, medida ponta a ponta

```
1.  kubelet  worker.go:296   "Non-running container probed"  pod=kube-system/etcd-…
                                                              22:03:30, :31, :32
2.  CRI      StopContainer  container=cri-3ebbc670d4bb182a    22:03:38.364034
3.  etcd     osutil/interrupt_unix.go:65
             "received signal; shutting down..."              22:03:38.421763
4.  etcd     sai 0 (encerramento ordeiro)
5.  apiserver  F hooks.go:203  PostStartHook
             "priority-and-fairness-config-producer" failed   → exit status 1
6.  scheduler / controller-manager
             "Unable to connect to the server: unexpected EOF" → CrashLoopBackOff
```

**57 ms** entre o passo 2 e o passo 3. O `cri-3ebbc670d4bb182a` é o contentor do `etcd` — confirmado pela coluna `NAMES` do `delonix container ps -a`, cujo `COMMAND` é `etcd --advertise-cli…`.

O passo 5 e o 6 são consequência: o apiserver morre por perder o etcd, e os outros dois por perderem o apiserver.

## O ponto de partida é o passo 1

O kubelet acredita que o contentor **não está a correr** e, por isso, manda pará-lo. O `StopContainer` é uma chamada gRPC que só o kubelet faz, portanto o remetente do sinal está identificado; o que falta explicar é **porque é que ele acredita nisso**.

## O que está medido

| | |
|---|---|
| ritmo | 125 → 126 reinícios totais em 75 s |
| disponibilidade | 4 amostras de minuto a minuto, apiserver **indisponível nas 4** |
| intermitência | noutra janela, `etcd` esteve `Up 3 minutos` com o processo vivo e zero queixas |
| nós | `Ready` os dois, durante tudo isto |
| `computePodActions` | `KillPod: false` para `etcd` (×20) e `kube-apiserver` (×17) — a paragem **não** vem por aí |

O último ponto importa: o kubelet não está a decidir `KillPod`. A paragem entra por outro caminho, e o `"Non-running container probed"` é o único candidato que aparece no jornal.

## A hipótese, e o que falta para a confirmar

Se o processo do `etcd` estiver **vivo** no instante em que o kubelet o dá como não-corrente, então é o `ContainerStatus` do CRI a reportar mal o estado — a mesma família do #233, que corrigiu o `PodSandboxStatus`, mas noutro RPC.

**Não confirmei isso.** Observei os dois estados, nunca no mesmo segundo. A alternativa continua viva: o contentor podia estar mesmo parado nesse instante, por uma razão anterior que não observei.

O que fecharia a questão, e não corri:

```bash
# no nó, durante um ciclo — capturar os dois no MESMO segundo
while :; do
  date +%T
  pgrep -f '^etcd --advertise' >/dev/null && echo "  processo VIVO" || echo "  processo MORTO"
  journalctl -u kubelet --since -1s | grep -c 'Non-running container probed.*etcd'
  sleep 1
done
```

Se aparecer `processo VIVO` na mesma linha de tempo em que o kubelet conta uma sonda de contentor não-corrente, a hipótese fica provada.

## Ambiente

Golden `delonix-vm-k8s:1.36-motor2` (`delonix 2.0.0`, commit `4eaf44355`), Kubernetes **1.36.4**, backend libvirt, 1 control-plane + 1 worker, kubelet com `--v=4`. Medido a 2026-09-07.

O cluster de teste está de pé e disponível para quem quiser correr a captura acima.

comments.body: Corrigido na main: #315 (705fc5ff). O CRI passa a anunciar `cgroupfs` ao kubelet (`engine_cgroup_driver()`), em vez de deixar o driver `systemd` criar slices vazios que perdiam o `cpuset` — a causa dos kills do etcd. Teste `the_kubelet_is_told_cgroupfs` verde no HEAD 85c19674. A prova com kubelet real (`/livez` estável, 0 StopContainer) está registada no #315; não foi repetida agora.

issues.body:
Uma correcção do `delonix-cri` **não chega a um nó existente**. O instalador pergunta se há um CRI a correr, não se está lá o CRI certo:

```rust
// cmd/cluster.rs, prepare_host()
if !remote::ssh_check(target, "systemctl is-active --quiet delonix-cri") {
    remote::scp_to(target, cri_bin, "/tmp/delonix-cri")?;
    remote::ssh_run(target, "mv /tmp/delonix-cri /usr/local/bin/delonix-cri && …")?;
    // … instala o serviço e faz `enable --now`
}
```

A golden traz o `delonix-cri` **e** o serviço ligado. Logo o `is-active` acerta, o bloco inteiro é saltado, e o binário da imagem ganha sempre — por mais recente que seja o que o `resolve_cri_bin` escolheu.

## O que isto custa

Medido a 2026-09-07, a validar uma correcção do CRI (#237/#239). Três tentativas gastas antes de encontrar a linha:

| tentativa | o que fiz | porque não funcionou |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | instalei o CRI corrigido no host | o `cluster kubeadm` não o usa se a imagem já tem um activo |
| 2 | dei-o ao `cluster kubeadm` | esse comando nem aceita `--cri-bin` — chama `resolve_cri_bin(None)` |
| 3 | pu-lo ao lado do `delonix` invocado, para o passo 2 do `resolve_cri_bin` o encontrar | o `resolve_cri_bin` **nunca é consultado**: está atrás deste `if` |

Só reconstruindo a golden — o passo que ninguém quer dar para testar uma linha — é que o binário chega.

## Porque é que isto é um problema de entrega, e não só de conveniência

Uma correcção do runtime fica **presa** até alguém reconstruir imagens. Num cluster já entregue a um cliente não há caminho nenhum: nem `delonix cluster` actualiza, nem existe comando que o faça.

E o efeito silencioso é pior do que a inconveniência: um operador que instale o binário novo, corra o `cluster kubeadm` e veja o cluster subir **acredita, com razão, que o nó tem o binário que ele instalou**. Não tem. Não há aviso nenhum.

## O que se esperaria

Comparar antes de decidir — versão, `sha256`, ou ambos — e substituir quando diferirem, em vez de perguntar apenas se algo está vivo. E, no mínimo, **dizer** qual dos dois ficou quando são diferentes: um instalador que salta em silêncio é a falha que este repo já persegue noutros sítios.

## Não validado

Não medi o que acontece quando o `is-active` falha e o bloco corre — presumo que instala correctamente, mas não o exercitei. E não li se existe outro caminho de actualização do CRI fora do `prepare_host`.

Medido contra `origin/main` (`7e67c6dd`), `delonix 2.0.0`, backend libvirt.

comments.body: Corrigido em 5eb622d3 (fundido em main, ainda sem tag): o `prepare_host` compara o sha256 do CRI do nó com o resolvido (`cri_action`) — igual e vivo não faz nada, igual e parado arranca, diferente substitui, faz `restart` e avisa. Testes: `the_binary_decides_before_the_service` (verde em main). Não validado contra um nó real por SSH.

issues.body:
Quando não encontra um `delonix-cri` ao lado do `delonix` em execução, o `resolve_cri_bin` **compila-o a partir do código-fonte que estiver perto do `cwd`**:

```rust
pub(crate) fn resolve_cri_bin(explicit: Option<PathBuf>) -> Result<PathBuf> {
    if let Some(p) = explicit { … }                     // 1. flag explícita
    if let Ok(exe) = std::env::current_exe() {          // 2. ao lado do binário
        let candidate = exe.parent()?.join("delonix-cri");
        if candidate.exists() { return Ok(candidate); }
    }
    if let Some(workspace_root) = find_workspace_root() {   // 3. compila do cwd
        eprintln!("compiling delonix-cri (release) from {dir}...");
        Command::new("cargo").args(["build", …
    }
}
```

O passo 3 faz do **directório de trabalho de quem corre o comando** a fonte do runtime que vai para os nós de um cluster.

## Como isto acontece sem ninguém escolher

Instalação normal, medida a 2026-09-07:

```
delonix                      /usr/local/bin/delonix
/usr/local/bin/delonix-cri   NÃO EXISTE
~/.local/bin/delonix-cri     10 872 896 bytes  (asset da release v2.0.0)
```

O passo 2 procura `/usr/local/bin/delonix-cri` — que não existe, porque o `install.sh` e a instalação manual não põem os dois lado a lado. Cai no passo 3.

Resultado observado num cluster: o binário nos nós tinha **12 882 208 bytes** — uma build local, não o asset de 10 872 896 que estava instalado na máquina. Ninguém pediu isso e nada o anunciou além de uma linha de `eprintln!` no meio da saída.

## Porque é que isto é grave e não só estranho

É a falha que a nossa própria doutrina de entrega regista como incidente de produção:

> «até 2026-08-20, a produção instalava **o que estivesse na árvore de trabalho de quem corria o playbook**. Correram-se binários de 15-08 que não correspondiam a commit nenhum. Isso não é uma release — é uma alteração não registada em produção.»

Aqui é o mesmo, do lado do motor, e o resultado é idêntico: **o runtime de um cluster não corresponde a commit nenhum publicado**, e não há como saber qual foi depois do facto. Se a árvore estiver suja — e neste workspace estão quase sempre — o binário nem sequer é reproduzível.

## O que se esperaria

O passo 3 é uma conveniência de desenvolvimento válida, mas não devia ser silencioso nem ser o comportamento por omissão fora de um checkout deliberado. As opções que fariam sentido, por ordem de preferência:

1. **Recusar** e dizer o que falta, quando o comando cria um cluster (por oposição a um teste local): «não encontrei `delonix-cri` ao lado de `/usr/local/bin/delonix`; instala-o ou passa `--cri-bin`».
2. **Carimbar a proveniência** — imprimir commit e `sha256` do que foi compilado, e registá-lo com o cluster.
3. **Deixar o `cluster kubeadm` aceitar `--cri-bin`**, que hoje não aceita; só o `image --vm build` o aceita.

## Relacionado

O #242 explica porque é que, na prática, nem o passo 3 chega aos nós quando a golden já traz um CRI activo. Os dois juntos fazem com que a origem do runtime de um cluster seja difícil de prever e de auditar.

## Não validado

Não confirmei se o passo 3 é alcançado noutros caminhos além do `cluster kubeadm`, nem li o `find_workspace_root` para saber a partir de que profundidade do `cwd` ele encontra um workspace.

comments.body: Corrigido em 5eb622d3 (fundido em main, ainda sem tag): compilar do cwd só com `DELONIX_CRI_FROM_SOURCE=1`; por omissão usa o `delonix-cri` ao lado do `delonix` e depois o asset verificado da release; a proveniência (origem, caminho, sha256) é sempre impressa; `cluster apply` e `cluster kubeadm` ganham `--cri-bin`. Teste: `building_cri_from_the_cwd_needs_an_explicit_opt_in` (verde em main).

issues.body:
## Objectivo

`delonix` (motor, CRI, MCP, mgmt) a compilar, testar, ser publicado e a correr em **linux/aarch64**, com a mesma garantia de gate que o x86_64 tem hoje. Sucede ao #414 (fechado sem resolver a causa de fundo) e retoma o que o PR #431 propunha (fechado por ter sido aberto antes de ser pedido).

Ordem já decidida no ADR-0018: **artefactos de release arm64 primeiro, imagens de VM arm64 depois** (as imagens VM ficam amd64 por agora, ver `docs/adr/0018-vm-images-stay-amd64.md`).

## Estado medido (`origin/main`, 2026-09-20)

Já é arch-aware (não refazer): tabela de syscalls do seccomp (#101), `close_range` por número (#87), selecção de plataforma OCI (`registry::target_arch`, `image::` e `build::` mapeiam `aarch64→arm64`), mensagem de falha de `cpu.max` sem delegação (#415).

## Lacunas

### 1. CI: nenhum job corre em arm64
- `grep aarch64|arm64 .github/workflows` → zero. As ramificações `#[cfg(target_arch)]` nunca são executadas por ninguém. Uma cross-build só type-checka; é preciso runner nativo (`ubuntu-24.04-arm`) com **build + suite completa**.
- Gate a sério, sem `continue-on-error`.

### 2. Release só publica x86_64
- `.github/workflows/release.yml` copia/assina apenas `delonix{,-cri,-mcp,-mgmt}-x86_64[-v3]-linux`.
- Falta job aarch64 (build, strip, verificação de `--version`) e incluir os 4 binários no mesmo `SHA256SUMS`, assinatura minisign e proveniência SLSA.
- A variante `-v3` é só x86; em arm64 há um único binário por componente.

### 3. `scripts/install.sh` recusa tudo o que não é x86_64
- L183-184: `[ "$ARCH" = x86_64 ] || die "no prebuilt binary for $ARCH yet"`.
- L358-371: nome do asset fixo `-x86_64${CPU_VARIANT}-linux`; a detecção de `-v3` (AVX2/BMI2/FMA) tem de ficar condicionada a x86.
- L725: sonda de QEMU pede `qemu-system-x86_64` — em arm64 reporta QEMU em falta e instala o emulador x86 errado (deve ser `qemu-system-aarch64`).

### 4. Código com x86 fixo
- `crates/adapters/delonix-sdn/build.rs:32,34`: `-D__TARGET_ARCH_x86` e `-I/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu` na compilação do objecto BPF. Em arm64 o build falha **em silêncio** (o `build.rs` engole o erro e o datapath eBPF sai sem existir). Derivar de `CARGO_CFG_TARGET_ARCH` (`__TARGET_ARCH_arm64`, multiarch dir por arch).
- `crates/adapters/delonix-vm/src/lib.rs:2711,2758,3330`: `<type arch='x86_64'>`, `<emulator>/usr/bin/qemu-system-x86_64`, e a sonda `available()` do backend libvirt. Em arm64 o domínio libvirt não é válido (`aarch64`, machine `virt`, UEFI/AAVMF obrigatório, sem VGA/`hvm` legacy).
- `crates/adapters/delonix-linux/src/cdi.rs`: caminhos `libcuda` em `x86_64-linux-gnu` (`aarch64-linux-gnu` em arm64; só afecta GPU).
- `bins/delonix-runtime-bin/src/cmd/vmimage.rs`: nomes de cloud image e `node_exporter` `amd64`/`x86_64` (fica coberto pelo ADR-0018 enquanto as imagens VM forem amd64, mas o erro tem de ser explícito em arm64, não um 404).
- Firmware do Cloud Hypervisor (`CLOUDHV.fd`/`hypervisor-fw`) é x86; em arm64 é outro artefacto.

### 5. Validação em runtime nunca feita fora do x86
- O #414 (aarch64, kernel 7.0 orbstack, root) chegou a `cgroup limit … cpu.max: Permission denied`. A causa era `cpu` não delegado (mensagem entretanto corrigida), mas **não há evidência de um `container run` completo em arm64** — rede SDN, overlay (`fsopen`/`fsconfig`), seccomp real, `exec`, CRI.

## Critérios de aceitação

- [ ] Job `test-arm64` nativo (`ubuntu-24.04-arm`): `cargo build --workspace` + `cargo test --workspace` verdes, sem `continue-on-error`.
- [ ] `release.yml` publica os 4 binários aarch64, incluídos em SHA256SUMS + minisign + SLSA.
- [ ] `install.sh` instala em aarch64 (verificação de checksum incluída) e a sonda de QEMU usa o binário certo.
- [ ] `delonix-sdn/build.rs` sem arch fixa; se o BPF não compilar, **avisa** em vez de calar.
- [ ] Backend libvirt gera XML válido para aarch64 (ou recusa com erro que diga porquê).
- [ ] Prova ao vivo num host arm64 real: `container run` (rootless e root), `--net <custom>`, `-p`, `exec`, `--privileged`, e `serve cri` contra o `crictl`. Relatório com o que ficou provado **e** o que não foi.
- [ ] `docs/` e README a dizerem a matriz de arquitecturas suportada.

## Fora de âmbito
Imagens VM arm64 (ADR-0018), variante `-v3`, macOS/Windows (ADR-0036).

**`delonix --version`**

```
delonix 4.5.0
commit: 7b1a766f8 · built: 2026-09-28 · Apache-2.0
```

**Environment**
- Distro / kernel version: `Linux delonix 7.0.0-38-generic #38~24.04.4-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Mon Sep 14 16:37:11 UTC 2 x86_64 GNU/Linux`
- Rootless or root: rootless (daemonless) — `delonix system info` → `mode: rootless (daemonless)`, `cgroup2 delegated: yes`
- Installed via: binary at `/usr/local/bin/delonix` (not re-verified install method, host already provisioned)

**What did you run?**

```
# 1. control-plane + 2 workers, kind-mode, no Docker
delonix cluster create --name delonix --workers 2

# 2. direct pod-to-pod connectivity test, same podCIDR, no NAT involved
#    (ping repeated from inside one pod to another pod's IP, both on nodes
#    managed by the same `dlx-delonix` network)
kubectl run pingtest --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sleep 3600
kubectl exec pingtest -- ping -c 5 <other-pod-ip>

# 3. control test: recreated single-node to isolate node count as the variable
delonix cluster destroy delonix --force
delonix cluster create --name delonix --workers 0
# repeated the same pod-to-pod test → 0% packet loss, 5/5

# 4. follow-up (single-node, days later, same cluster instance): first-time
#    cross-NAMESPACE connections from freshly scheduled pods, via a Kubernetes
#    Service ClusterIP, time out — even with the destination's NetworkPolicy
#    egress rule set to fully open (`egress: [{}]`, no restriction at all)
kubectl run netpol-test --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -- \
  curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "HTTP_CODE=%{http_code}\n" --max-time 8 \
  http://some-service.other-namespace.svc.cluster.local:8080/
# → curl: (28) Connection timed out after 8002ms, 5/5 attempts, 0% success
```

**What did you expect to happen?**

Reliable pod-to-pod connectivity regardless of node count (multi-node) or
namespace (single-node, first connection from a freshly scheduled pod),
matching standard `kind`/kubeadm behavior on Docker.

**What actually happened?**

Two related but distinct symptoms, both pointing at the same underlying area
(the routing/forwarding fabric between node containers / for freshly created
pods), traced over two sessions on the same `delonix`-managed cluster:

1. **Multi-node (2+ workers): pod-to-pod is almost entirely broken.**
   - Node→node direct connectivity (curl/ping from inside a node's own
     netns, outside any pod) to another node's `:6443` and to the service VIP
     `10.96.0.1:443`: always fast (4–6ms). Rules out node-to-node network
     hardware/bridge issues.
   - Pod→VIP from inside a pod: **first attempt always succeeds**, every
     subsequent attempt from the *same* pod **times out completely** (no
     SYN-ACK, `time_connect=0`).
   - Ruled out double-masquerade (`KIND-MASQ-AGENT` re-masquerading traffic
     already masqueraded by `KUBE-POSTROUTING`): added
     `iptables -t nat -I KIND-MASQ-AGENT 1 -d 10.247.0.0/16 -j RETURN` on all
     3 nodes — no change.
   - Decisive test: **pod-to-pod ping on the *same* node** (no NAT, same
     podCIDR, local bridge only) — **100% packet loss**, including the very
     first attempt (not just subsequent ones).
   - Control test: recreated the cluster **single-node**
     (`--workers 0`) — same pod-to-pod test: **0% packet loss, 5/5**.
     This isolates the defect to the inter-node fabric specifically
     (the `dlx-delonix` network between node containers), not pod
     networking in general.

2. **Single-node, days later, same cluster: first-time cross-namespace
   connections from freshly scheduled pods also fail**, with a notably
   similar signature (works once established / for long-running pods, fails
   for brand-new connection attempts):
   - Long-running pods with an already-established traffic pattern keep
     working fine (e.g. an Envoy Gateway pod that's been proxying to a
     backend Service for ~75 minutes continues to work without issue).
   - A **brand-new pod** (`kubectl run ... --rm`) making its **first**
     connection to a Service in a **different namespace** times out
     consistently — 5/5 attempts, every fresh pod.
   - Confirmed this is unrelated to `NetworkPolicy` content/scope: tested
     with the destination's egress policy completely removed in favor of a
     fully permissive one (`egress: [{}]`, no namespaceSelector, no port
     restriction) — **still times out**. Also confirmed same-namespace
     traffic (both Service-ClusterIP and direct pod-IP) from a fresh pod in
     the *same* namespace as the target works fine and fast.
   - This suggests the fault may not be strictly multi-node-only — possibly
     the same routing-setup-for-new-pod/new-conntrack-entry class of bug,
     with the single-node mitigation only reducing (not eliminating) the
     blast radius down to specifically *new* cross-namespace flows.

**Can you reproduce it reliably?**
- [x] Yes, every time (for both symptoms, each within their respective
  scenario — multi-node pod-to-pod, and single-node first-time
  cross-namespace from a fresh pod)

**Anything else that might be relevant?**

- Both scenarios run through `kindnet` (the CNI bundled in
  `kindest/node:v1.34.0`) — Cilium was evaluated as an alternative CNI but is
  currently blocked by a separate, unrelated issue on this same host
  (`RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` cannot be raised from inside a userns-remapped node
  container without `CAP_SYS_RESOURCE` on the real host root — a rootless
  design constraint, not a delonix bug per se, happy to file separately if
  useful).
- `NetworkPolicy` enforcement itself (via kindnet) is otherwise confirmed
  working correctly in this cluster for established/already-working rule
  shapes (default-deny, same-namespace allow, ingress-from-another-namespace
  with and without a port restriction) — this report is specifically about
  connectivity itself (not policy enforcement) for (a) multi-node pod-to-pod
  and (b) first-time cross-namespace flows from freshly scheduled pods.
- Full write-up with the complete multi-node diagnosis (point 1) was done in
  an earlier session; point 2 is a new data point from a follow-up session on
  the same cluster, added for anyone else hitting the same class of issue
  while believing single-node mode fully resolves it.

| test | result |
|---|---|
| same node, `p0 → p0b`, 5 pings | 0% loss (the report had 100%) |
| across nodes, `p0 → p1`, 5 pings | 0% loss |
| across nodes, `p1 → p2`, 5 pings | 0% loss |
| across nodes, `p0 → p2`, 20 pings at 0.2 s | 0% loss |
| ONE pod making 6 consecutive connections to a `ClusterIP` (the report: first OK, the rest time out) | 6/6 OK, same namespace and cross-namespace |

|---|---|

issues.body:
Follow-up to #736 — that issue has the symptoms and reproduction steps; this
one is a proposed debugging/fix plan, since the root cause was never
confirmed (only several hypotheses ruled out: double-masquerade, mount vs.
memlock for the unrelated BLOQ-01). Both symptoms in #736 share a signature —
**new** connections/flows fail, **established** ones keep working — which
narrows the search considerably. Ranked by how well that signature fits:

### 1. ARP/FDB learning race on the bridge for newly-attached veths (most likely)

If a new pod's veth is attached to the node's bridge (or the `dlx-delonix`
inter-node bridge, for the multi-node case) but the bridge's FDB / the
peer's ARP cache hasn't learned the new MAC/IP yet, the first packet(s) can
silently black-hole until something triggers learning (a broadcast, a GARP,
or ARP resolution timing out and retrying). This fits "first pod-to-pod ping
on the same node: 100% packet loss, including the very first attempt" from
#736 — not just "works once then breaks," but genuinely never establishes if
nothing ever triggers the learn.

**To test:**
```
# right after scheduling a new pod that will fail its first cross-ns/cross-node call:
ip netns exec <node-netns> bridge fdb show | grep <new-pod-veth-mac>
ip netns exec <node-netns> ip neigh show | grep <new-pod-ip>
# does delonix send a gratuitous ARP when it brings the veth up? grep the engine's
# veth/bridge-attach code path for anything calling arping/send_garp or equivalent
# does manually priming it fix the very first connection?
ip netns exec <pod-netns> arping -c 1 -I eth0 <default-gw-ip>
# then immediately retry the curl that was timing out
```
If priming the ARP/neigh entry before the real traffic fixes it, the engine's
veth-attach sequence needs to either send a GARP on attach or pre-populate
the neighbor table, instead of relying on lazy resolution.

### 2. rp_filter (strict reverse-path filtering) dropping asymmetric first packets

Common cause of "first SYN just vanishes, no RST, no ICMP" on exactly this
kind of multi-bridge/multi-netns topology, especially if the return path for
a brand-new flow briefly differs from the forward path before routes/conntrack
settle.

**To test:**
```
sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter
# per-interface too, for the bridge + veth + any dlx-delonix uplink:
for i in /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/*/rp_filter; do echo "$i: $(cat $i)"; done
# if any relevant interface is at 1 (strict), test with it set to 2 (loose) or 0:
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.<iface>.rp_filter=2
# retry the failing connection
```

### 3. conntrack entry not created / wrong zone for the first packet

**To test:**
```
# tail conntrack during a failing attempt
conntrack -E &
<run the failing curl>
# look for the SYN_SENT entry — does it appear at all, does it ever flip to
# ESTABLISHED, does it get created in a conntrack zone the return path isn't
# looking at (relevant if delonix uses network namespaces + veth pairs with
# per-zone conntrack for its rootless networking model)
conntrack -L | grep <pod-ip>
```

### 4. A readiness race in the veth/route bring-up sequence itself

If delonix marks a pod "running" and lets kubelet/CNI report Ready before the
host-side veth + routes + iptables rules for it are fully programmed, the
pod's very first outbound packet can race the setup. This would also explain
why established pods (already past that window) keep working fine, and why
single-node mode reduces but doesn't eliminate it (shorter/fewer hops still
has *a* window, multi-node just has more of them to fall into).

**To test:** add a deliberate `sleep 2` (or poll `ip route get` until the
expected route appears) right after pod start, before the first real request
— if that reliably "fixes" it, it's a race, not a permanent block, and the
real fix is making pod-ready gate on network-ready, not just
container-started.

### Suggested next step

Whichever of the above reproduces/explains it, the actual fix almost
certainly lives in delonix's pod network setup path (wherever the veth pair,
bridge attach, and initial routes/ARP get programmed for a new pod) — happy
to help narrow further with `delonix system events`/`net flow -w` output
captured live during a failing first-connection attempt, if that's useful
context to attach here.

## Summary

The published `delonix-vm-k8s` golden images under tags `1.34` and `1.36`
(`ghcr.io/angolardevops/delonix-vm-k8s`) do not boot — they drop into GRUB
rescue mode (`error: no such partition`) instead of reaching the kernel.
A locally built image from the same recipe boots cleanly in under a
minute, so the defect is in the publish pipeline (`vm-image.yml`), not in
the image recipe (`delonix image vm build --offline`) itself.

## Evidence

1. **The two published tags are byte-identical.** SHA-256 of the qcow2
   blob behind `:1.34` and `:1.36` matches exactly, after `delonix vm pull`
   of each into an isolated `DELONIX_ROOT`/`DELONIX_NET_RUNTIME_DIR`. Two
   builds with different `--k8s-version` values producing the same bytes
   means one tag's build overwrote the other's — the publish workflow is
   not producing (or is not uploading) a distinct artifact per version.
2. **Both fail to boot, reproduced two independent ways:**
   - Plain `qemu-system-x86_64` against the pulled qcow2 — GRUB rescue
     shell, `error: no such partition`. Rules out any delonix runtime code
     (rootless netns, cloud-hypervisor, slirp) as the cause: this is QEMU
     with no delonix process involved.
   - A real `delonix vm create --backend libvirt` domain from the same
     pulled image — identical symptom on the console.
   - `qemu-img check` on the qcow2 reports no corruption — the blob itself
     is structurally fine; the GRUB/bootloader contents inside it are
     wrong.
3. **A locally built image from the exact same recipe works.** Running
   `delonix image vm build --offline --k8s-version 1.36 -t
   delonix-vm-k8s:1.36-local` on a clean host produces a 895.9 MiB qcow2
   that:
   - boots to a login prompt under plain QEMU + KVM in well under a
     minute (confirmed via serial console log, not just exit code);
   - was used end-to-end to bootstrap a real 2-node `kubeadm` cluster
     (`delonix cluster kubeadm --control-plane 1 --workers 1`) with the
     control-plane and CNI-wired worker both reaching `Ready`, running a
     real workload (an `nginx` Deployment) scheduled on the worker's
     kubelet, reachable via ClusterIP from a pod on the other node.

   The local build's `virt-customize` log shows it running
   `grub-install --target=i386-pc /dev/sda && update-grub` as one of the
   last steps before `compacting the image` — this step (or its output)
   is the most likely place for the published artifact to have diverged
   from what was actually tested/intended.

## Likely root cause

Something in `.github/workflows/vm-image.yml` is either:
- re-running the build for `1.36` against stale/cached state from the
  `1.34` run and uploading the wrong qcow2 under both tags, or
- the `qemu-img convert -c -o compression_type=zstd` / sparsify step (see
  AGENTS.md "Tamanho do artefacto") truncating or corrupting the GRUB boot
  sector/partition table on the path that runs in CI but not locally
  (different `qemu-img`/`libguestfs` version on the runner image?).

Given the two tags are byte-identical, the first hypothesis (same blob
pushed to both tags) is the stronger lead — worth checking the workflow's
actual run logs for the two `k8s_version` dispatches to see if they
produced genuinely different artifacts before upload.

## What this blocks

Anyone running `delonix vm pull` (or `cluster kubeadm --vm-image
delonix-vm-k8s:1.34|1.36` without a local image already present) gets an
unbootable VM with no indication anything is wrong until they look at the
console — `vm create`/`cluster kubeadm` both report success because the
VMM process starts fine; only the guest fails.

## Suggested next step

Re-run `vm-image.yml` for `1.36` with `workflow_dispatch`, diff the
resulting qcow2's SHA-256 against what's currently published, and check
the run logs for the `grub-install`/`update-grub` and the
sparsify/compress steps specifically. If the new artifact differs and
boots, replace both published tags (they should not have been identical
in the first place).

## Not in scope here

This repo (`delonix-runtime`) only contains the recipe and the workflow
definition — this issue is about the *result* of running that workflow,
which is outside what a code change here can fix. Filed so whoever
re-runs/triages the publish step has the full repro in one place.

comments.body:
Closing: the published `delonix-vm-k8s` golden images boot, and the 1.36 one forms a working kubeadm cluster. Evidence below, measured 2026-10-11.

## What was wrong

The tags were published before `vm-image.yml` had a boot probe (`scripts/vm_boot_probe.sh`, SeaBIOS + OVMF before push). All three tags were rebuilt and republished from `8605dab0`, each through the probe:

| tag | run | result |
|---|---|---|
| `1.36` | 38090529241 | success, boot probe passed |
| `1.35` | 38090532577 | success, boot probe passed |
| `1.34` | 38090538286 | success, boot probe passed |

## End-to-end validation (published image + published release)

Isolated `DELONIX_ROOT`, `DELONIX_NET_RUNTIME_DIR`, `HOME` and `KUBECONFIG`, libvirt backend. Release **v5.0.2** binaries, verified by sha256, minisign (key from `scripts/install.sh` on main) and commit `152fccd8`.

1. The local copy was deleted, then pulled again. The qcow2 sha256 is the same as the registry's layer digest: `7ac420229c78a5056a34a8bc0d4f454fee98a13e508b36d8ee1f9ca65bea851e`.
2. `cluster kubeadm --name k753 --network k753 --control-plane 1 --workers 1 --vm-image delonix-vm-k8s:1.36`: `kubeadm init` in 18.2 s, worker joined in 6.5 s, `delonix://5.0.2` as the runtime, control-plane pods `Running` with 0 restarts.
3. The nodes went `Ready` after a CNI was applied by hand. The kubeadm path installs a CNI only for a single-node cluster; tracked as #799.
4. `nginx:alpine` ran on the worker behind a `ClusterIP` Service. A busybox pod pinned to the control-plane fetched `http://web.default.svc.cluster.local` across the nodes and got `<title>Welcome to nginx!</title>`.

## Corrections and side findings

- **The «byte-identical» claim in this issue was wrong.** The `1.34` and `1.36` tags did not have the same layer digest. The real cause was the missing boot probe at publish time, not one blob pushed under two tags.
- On the way, main had a CRI regression: a `hugetlb` limit of 0 for an empty pool was refused, so no control-plane container could start. Fixed in #787. Neither v5.0.1 nor v5.0.2 contains the commit that introduced it (`f72a4f55`).
- One validation run failed because `cluster kubeadm` replaces the node's `delonix-cri` with the one next to the operator's `delonix`. That binary was built before #787, so the fixed one on the image was overwritten. Running with matching release binaries removed the problem. This is by design, but worth knowing when validating an image against a dev build.
- Another run had both VMs paused (`paused (I/O error)`) when the host's root filesystem filled up. This was environmental: resumed with `virsh resume`, the cluster continued without restarts.

## Not validated

- 1.35 and 1.34 were checked by the CI boot probe only, not with a kubeadm cluster.
- Multi-control-plane (HA) was not exercised.

issues.body:
## Summary

Two related defects in `crates/interfaces/delonix-node-api/src/operations.rs`, found by a
line-by-line review and reproduced against the real code (commit `2b9087b0`, v5.0.0, `tests/
achado_a_operation_race.rs` and `tests/achado_b_idempotent_identity.rs` in the review branch):

1. **Concurrency**: `operations::begin()`'s exclusive-creation staging file is not unique per
   *attempt* (only per `(request_id, pid)`), so two threads racing the same `request_id` —
   ordinary behaviour of any client retry under `tokio::spawn_blocking`, which every mutation
   goes through with zero serialization above it — share one staging inode. Measured: **33–40%
   of racing retries get a hard `Internal`/ENOENT error instead of the clean replay ADR-0042
   promises** ("the same request sent again is answered with that operation").
2. **Identity**: `operations::replay()` decides "is this the same request?" by comparing only
   `(verb, target)`, where `target` is just the resource's bare name
   (`format!("VirtualMachine/{name}")` / `format!("Network/{name}")`). A `request_id` reused
   across two requests that differ in `spec` (image, vcpus, memory, namespace, …) is silently
   answered with the FIRST request's `Operation` — the second request's distinct content never
   reaches validation or the work closure.

Full analysis, line numbers, and the alternatives considered: `docs/adr/0076-operation-ledger-
race-identity-and-vm-image-defaults.md`, Context sections A and B, Decision D1/D2.

## Reproduction

### Finding 1 (race)

```
cargo test -p delonix-node-api --test achado_a_operation_race -- --nocapture --test-threads=1
```

Two threads call `begin(root, "create", "Network/lab", &same_request_id)` behind a
`std::sync::Barrier`, repeated 1500 times with a fresh `request_id` each iteration. Expected:
every pair resolves to exactly one `Begun::New` and one `Begun::Replay`. Observed (two
independent runs): `New=1500, Replay=911, Err=589` and `New=1500, Replay=999, Err=501` — i.e.
33–40% of the non-executing thread in each pair gets:

```
status: Internal, message: "operation record: creating: No such file or directory (os error 2)"
```

### Finding 2 (identity)

```
cargo test -p delonix-node-api --test achado_b_idempotent_identity -- --nocapture --test-threads=1
```

`create_with_fn` (the crate's own injectable test seam) called twice with the same
`request_id="same-key"`, `name="web"`, but request 1 is `image="alpine:a", vcpus=2,
memory=2048M` and request 2 is `image="ubuntu:b", vcpus=16, memory=65536M`. The work closure —
which would realize the VM — is recorded as called exactly **once**, with request 1's content;
`op1.id == op2.id`. The client of request 2 is told "succeeded" describing a VM it did not ask
for.

## Root cause

**Finding 1**: `operations.rs:236`, `std::fs::write(&staged, bytes)` opens the existing path
`.{id}.{pid}.new` in place (truncate, same inode) rather than creating a fresh one, because the
staged name has no per-attempt uniqueness. `delonix_node::write_atomic_mode`
(`crates/contexts/delonix-node/src/atomic.rs:21-33`) already names this exact failure mode in
its own doc comment and fixes it with a `pid + sequence` suffix; `operations::begin()`'s staging
path predates or missed that discipline.

**Finding 2**: `operations.rs:267`, `found.verb != verb || found.target != target` is the entire
identity check. `target` carries only the resource name (`network_ops.rs:209,251`,
`vm_ops.rs:345,385,469`) — nothing from the request body.

## Proposed fix

See ADR-0076, Decision D1 and D2:

- **D1**: stage at `.{id}.{pid}.{seq}.new` with a process-wide atomic sequence (reusing or
  mirroring `delonix_node::atomic`'s discipline). One-line change to the staged path, no change
  to the surrounding `hard_link`/`AlreadyExists`/`replay` logic.
- **D2**: `Record` gains `#[serde(default)] fingerprint: String`; each mutation computes a
  canonical, versioned fingerprint of its semantically-relevant fields (map-order-independent,
  omitted-equals-default) and passes it to `begin`/`replay`, which refuse a `(verb, target)`
  match whose fingerprint disagrees (a new, distinct error — not silently replayed, not silently
  treated as a second operation). An empty stored fingerprint (legacy records, or a mutation not
  yet updated) is not compared, bounded by `RETENTION_SECS` (7 days).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `achado_a_operation_race.rs`'s two tests pass at 0 hard errors across at least 1500
      iterations and a 12-thread wide race (or the equivalent coverage is folded into
      `operations.rs`'s own `#[cfg(test)]` module — this review's files are a reproduction, not
      necessarily the final test shape).

`vm_ops::config_from_spec` (`crates/interfaces/delonix-node-api/src/vm_ops.rs:176-184`) resolves
`spec.vcpus == 0` / `spec.memory_bytes == 0` to a fixed `(1 vCPU, 1 GiB)`, never consulting the

(`proto/delonix/node/v1/compute.proto:550-551`):

```proto
int32 vcpus = 2;        // 0 = image default, then 1
int64 memory_bytes = 3; // 0 = image default, then 1 GiB
```

and diverges from `bins/delonix-runtime-bin/src/cmd/vm.rs::resolve_vm_defaults`, which DOES
consult the image for the identical "nothing given" case. The module's own doc comment already
names this as a known, deliberate gap, blocked on ADR-0040's layering rule (an interface crate
cannot depend on a bin crate, where `VmImageStore` lives today).

Full analysis: `docs/adr/0076-operation-ledger-race-identity-and-vm-image-defaults.md`, Context
section C, Decision D3.

## Reproduction

```
cargo test -p delonix-node-api --test achado_c_vm_defaults -- --nocapture --test-threads=1
```

A fixture `<root>/vm-images/golden.json` is written in the exact shape and location
`VmImageStore::save` produces, recommending `default_vcpus: 4, default_memory: "4G"`.

node API, to `vcpus=1, memory="1G"` — the fixture is never read. The CLI's own existing,
unmodified test for the identical scenario corroborates the divergence:

```
cargo test -p delonix-runtime-bin resolve_vm_defaults_cai_para_a_imagem_quando_o_cli_nao_diz_nada
```

resolves the same input to `(4, "4G")`.

an image reference with no recorded metadata at all falls back to `(1, "1G")` in both (also not
the gap) — the divergence is specifically: image exists, has its own recorded defaults, request
says 0.

See ADR-0076, Decision D3: a minimal `ImageDefaults` port in `delonix_compute::ports` (three
fields: `vcpus`, `memory`, `backend` — not `VmImage`'s full build/registry metadata), wired via

`VmNetwork` (`set_network`/`network()`), implemented in `delonix-vm::local_ports` by reading
`<root>/vm-images/<name>.json`'s three optional fields directly — independent of `bins/delonix-
runtime-bin`'s `VmImageStore`, so no `interfaces`→`bins` dependency is introduced.

- [ ] `scripts/arch_fitness.py` stays green (no new disallowed crate-direction edge).

      limitations" flags this as unverified by this review).

ignored), and the only contract a caller has (the proto field comment) promises the opposite.

## Summary

A control plane reaches each node through a **node agent**: a small per-node process that terminates TLS with client certificates, decides which callers may reach the node, writes an audit line per call, and hands each call **unchanged** to this socket (`delonix serve node-api`). The agent does not interpret the contract: gRPC stays HTTP/2, REST stays HTTP/1.1, so every RPC this socket starts serving is reachable through the agent the same day.

This keeps the engine's guard-rails as they are (ADR-0010): the node API stays local, on a unix socket, with no remote clients and no caller identities. The agent is where remoteness lives.

What blocks the agent from replacing direct local access is what `delonix-node-api` does not serve yet. This issue lists it, measured against `main` at `d7347ac7` (2026-10-10).

## Served on `main` today

| Service | Served | Answers `unserved` |
|---|---|---|
| `NodeService` | `GetApiRoot`, `GetNodeInfo`, `GetHealth`, `GetCapacity`, `ListProviders` | `WatchEvents` |
| `NetworkService` | `GetNetwork`, `ListNetworks`, `CreateNetwork`, `DeleteNetwork` | `ConnectContainer`, `DisconnectContainer` |
| `VolumeService` | `GetVolume`, `ListVolumes` | `CreateVolume`, `DeleteVolume` |
| `VirtualMachineService` | everything except `Console` | `Console` |
| `OperationService` | `GetOperation`, `ListOperations` | `WatchOperation`, `CancelOperation` |
| `ContainerService`, `PodService`, `ImageService`, `StackService` | — | not registered |

## Requested, in order

1. **`ContainerService`, all of it**: create, get, list, update, delete, start, stop, kill, wait, `Exec`, `Logs`, `Stats`. Almost everything a control plane does to a node's workloads goes through it, and nothing of it is served.
2. **What is already in the contract but answers `unserved`**: `NetworkService.ConnectContainer` / `DisconnectContainer`, `VolumeService.CreateVolume` / `DeleteVolume`.
3. **Operations a control plane performs today that have no RPC in `delonix.node.v1`**, to be added to the contract:
   - pause and resume a container;
   - mount and unmount a volume into a running container;
   - set and clear a container's network bandwidth limit;
   - set a container's scheduling priority (nice);
   - add a peer to an overlay network;
   - publish and unpublish a VM port.
4. **`ImageService`**: pull, delete, scan.
5. **`WatchEvents`** and **`WatchOperation`**, so a caller can stop polling.

## Not asked

Nothing of tenants, quotas, admission or scheduling decisions: those stay above the engine. Nothing remote either — the socket stays local; the agent bridges it.

## How it is checked

The agent is tested against a fake node API and, live, against `delonix serve node-api` (4.5.0 on the dev host, which serves `GET /v1/providers`): REST over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 reach the engine and its answer comes back unchanged. Each RPC served here becomes usable through the agent without a change to it.

## Finding (security assessment)

The CRI capability ceiling (`crates/interfaces/delonix-cri/src/cap_ceiling.rs`) defaults to
**no ceiling** when `DELONIX_CRI_CAP_CEILING` is unset. Combined with the engine honouring
`seccomp: unconfined` and `cap_add` exactly as the kubelet asks, a node whose operator never
set the ceiling admits a pod with `privileged: true` (or `cap_add: [SYS_ADMIN, …]`) and grants
it full caps with no seccomp — a straightforward container escape to root on the node. A
`crictl`/kubelet talking straight to the socket bypasses any admission controller that lives in
another process/machine; the ceiling is the only **local** barrier and it is off by default.

**Root cause**: deliberate "unopinionated engine, consumer hardens" design decision — not a
code bug. A safe default is a minimum ceiling widened explicitly, not the inverse.

## Why this is an issue, not a patch

Flipping the default to `default` (the engine's `KEPT_CAPS`) changes the `serve cri` contract
and must ride a **major** release. Scope here is `delonix-runtime` only; the consumer-side
hardening test (`hardening_e2e.rs`) lives in `delonix-paas` and runs in no CI.

## Proposed, non-breaking now

- `serve cri` **warns loudly at startup** when no ceiling is set (stdout banner + `tracing::warn`),
  so an operator who never configured one is told, instead of discovering it after an escape.
- The default flip to a minimum ceiling is a separate decision tracked for the next major.

Found during the 2026-10-10 offensive audit. Sibling of #788 (decompression bomb, fixed).

## Finding (security assessment)

`cmd/remote.rs` connects with `StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new` (`conn_args`), and
`cluster apply` / `vm migrate` SSH into production hosts as root (`sudo -n bash -c …`). TOFU
means the **first** contact with a new host is trusted unconditionally: an attacker who can
MITM/ARP-spoof/DNS-spoof that first connection becomes the "known" host, captures the `sudo`
session and injects commands as root. The window is the first `cluster apply`; after that the
key is pinned.

**Root cause**: deliberate usability choice in `conn_args` — `ssh` (the external binary) does
exactly what it is told. Command injection itself is already closed (`shell_quote` + `--` +
the `valid_endpoint`/`valid_cidr`/`valid_version` validators from audit #1); this is only the
host-key trust.

## Proposed

- Let the operator pin trust: honour a `known_hosts` / expected fingerprint per host (env or
  manifest), defaulting to `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes` against it.
- At minimum, **surface the fingerprint** that `accept-new` just trusted, so a first contact is
  not silent.

Keep `accept-new` as the opt-in fallback for greenfield bootstraps. Touches sensitive remote
SSH plumbing — wants careful review. Found during the 2026-10-10 offensive audit.

issues.body:
## Finding (security assessment) — LOW, defense-in-depth

Layer extraction keeps setuid/setgid bits (`owners::unpack_recording`,
`set_preserve_permissions(true)`). The module comment argues this is safe **in rootless mode**:
the files are owned by the engine's uid, which is root *inside* the container's user namespace,
so a setuid bit grants nothing the invoking user lacks. That reasoning is correct for rootless.

On the **root / CRI path** (engine as real root, kubelet), a setuid-root binary planted in an
image layer is setuid-root on the node filesystem, inside the container's rootfs. It is only
exploitable combined with another primitive (a privileged pod, a bind-mount that exposes the
path), hence LOW.

## Why there is no clean patch

Dropping setuid/setgid on the root path **regresses ADR-0062**: that preservation exists
because `/tmp` came out `777` instead of `1777` and `su`/`ping`/`sudo` lost their bit inside
every container. A naive drop re-breaks legitimate setuid binaries in pods. Any mitigation here
has to distinguish "image-declared setuid the workload needs" from "planted escalation", which
the extractor cannot do alone.

This issue is to track the analysis, not to ship a risky change. The real mitigations stay the
existing ones: do not admit privileged pods, the default masked/readonly paths, and the cap
ceiling (#<issue2>). Found during the 2026-10-10 offensive audit.

comments.body:
Estreitado no PR #800 (merge 218335f5).

A metade que se consegue largar **sem** regredir o ADR-0062 está fechada: numa extracção como **root real** (euid 0 no userns inicial), um bit setuid de um ficheiro cujo dono é um **uid ≠ 0** é largado — é setuid a uma identidade nomeada do nó, que nenhum container precisa e que uma layer plantada usa para tomar um utilizador real da máquina. `sanitize_special_bits` (pura, testada sem ser root) decide; `unpack_recording` larga-o, `scan` não o repõe.

Ficam intactos (o container precisa deles): **setuid-root** (o `su`/`mount` da imagem), **setgid a qualquer grupo** (`wall`/`crontab`), **sticky** (`/tmp`), e o **caminho rootless inteiro** byte-a-byte.

**Residual, por desenho:** setuid-**root** de uma layer não confiável continua a ser preservado (largá-lo partiria o `su` nos pods). Fica mitigado pelos controlos já existentes — dirs de layer a 0700, sem pods privilegiados, os masked/readonly paths por omissão, e o tecto de capacidades (#789). Mantenho aberta como registo deste residual aceite.

Narrowed by #800: on the real-root extraction path, a setuid/setgid bit owned by a non-root uid is now dropped (it would be setuid to a named host identity, which no container needs). The setuid-root bits stay on purpose: they are what makes a pod's `su`, `mount`, `wall` and a sticky `/tmp` work (ADR-0062), and they are only exploitable combined with another primitive, as the finding says. The residual is accepted by the owner (2026-10-11); closing as not planned.

## Summary

When `StartContainer` fails, the CRI can report the engine's **progress line** as the reason, which hides the real cause. The kubelet event then shows a step that succeeded.

Measured on 2026-10-10 on a kubeadm node built from `delonix-vm-k8s:1.36` (k8s 1.36.4, root CRI), while validating #753:

```
E1010 21:17:52.076213 remote_runtime.go:435] "StartContainer from runtime service failed"
  err="rpc error: code = Internal desc = failed to start container 1feeb556fcf0cbb5: ✓ unpacking the image 📦 0.8s"
```

A second container failed with `• unpacking the image 📦` as its whole reason. The real cause in that run was found only by reading other containers' errors on the node (`cgroup limit: hugetlb.2MB.limit_in_bytes=0: the hugetlb controller is not delegated…`, fixed in #787).

## Cause

`delonix_detached_why_in` (`crates/interfaces/delonix-cri/src/runtime_svc/lifecycle.rs`) captures the engine's stderr to a file. When the command fails, it returns the **first line**:

```rust
// First line only: clap appends usage text, …
why.lines().next().unwrap_or(why).to_string()
```

`delonix __apirun` writes `output::Progress` lines (`• …`, `✓ … 0.8s`) to stderr before the error. On the non-TTY path these are plain lines, so the first line is the image-unpack step, not the `delonix: …` error that follows it.

The "first line" rule was written for clap usage text (#309/#320 era). It is wrong for any engine path that reports progress before it fails.

## What a fix needs

- Choose the reason line on purpose: prefer the line that starts with `delonix:` (the engine's error prefix). Otherwise use the last line that is not a progress line (`•`/`✓`/`✗`). Fall back to the exit status.
- Add a unit test with a captured stderr made of progress lines followed by the error. It must fail with the current first-line rule.
- The same helper serves `RunPodSandbox` (`delonix_detached_why`), so both callers get the fix.

## Not measured

- I did not recover the real cause of the two failures that showed only progress lines. Their stderr files had been removed. This is exactly the information the bug loses.

## Summary

Under host I/O saturation, a CRI container start can hit the 60 s ceiling of the «mounted» handshake (`wait_for_mounts`, `crates/adapters/delonix-linux/src/lib.rs`). The engine then warns and returns success:

```
✓ unpacking the image 📦 11.1s
delonix: warning: cri-68784787b0fb2c6b did not finish mounting within 60000ms — it is running, but a command that enters it right now may see the HOST's filesystem instead of the container's
```

Measured on 2026-10-10 on a kubeadm node (`delonix-vm-k8s:1.36`). Inside the VM, `/proc/pressure/io` showed `full` at ~93%, and a plain `run -d` of `pause` took 19–45 s. The warning appeared on two of four control-plane containers started in the same minute (`cri-68784787b0fb2c6b`, `cri-c4d7f21de43e1c86`).

## Why it matters

The ceiling is correct: an unbounded wait would hang the `run`. The outcome is `Unknown`, which by design is never read as a failure. But the CRI then answers `StartContainer` with **success**, so the kubelet sees a running container. Any `ExecSync` or probe that enters it in that window can run against the host's filesystem. This is the window that the post-v0.66 fix ("an exec right after `run -d` ran on the HOST") closed for the normal case. Here it only moves out to 60 s.

## Questions to decide (measured, not guessed)

1. Should the CRI treat `MountWait::Unknown` differently from the CLI? Options: keep waiting under the kubelet's own deadline, or report `StartContainer` as failed so the kubelet retries. Both change behaviour that the kubelet observes.
2. Should `exec` (and `ExecSync`) refuse while the container record has no «mounted» proof, instead of relying on the start-time wait? The record already only gets its `pid` after the proof in the normal path. In the `Unknown` path, is it saved before the proof?
3. Is 60 s the right ceiling for a node, or should it scale with the observed I/O pressure?

## Not measured

- Whether an `exec` actually landed on the host filesystem in this run. The warning says it *may*; no probe was taken.
- Behaviour on an idle host: the same image mounts in well under a second there.
issues.title: linux: a container that misses the 60 s mount ceiling under I/O saturation is reported as started

## Summary

A `container start` into a custom network reports a failure and tears down the network attachment, but the container's init is **alive**. The record says `Running` with an IP. The veth, the ref marker and the IPAM lease are gone. The container keeps running with only `lo`, and its address is free to be leased to the next container on the network.

Measured on 2026-10-11 with the published **v5.0.2** (`152fccd8`, verified by sha256 and minisign). Run: `delonix cluster create --name n736 --workers 2` (kind mode), rootless, isolated `DELONIX_ROOT`/`DELONIX_NET_RUNTIME_DIR`/`HOME`/`KUBECONFIG`, host calm at start (io full 7.9, load 7.1).

## What the CLI said

```
delonix: system call `container start` failed: n736-worker2: the container's init exited with code 126 before its root filesystem was ready, so the container is not running: INFO: detected IPv4 address: 10.229.26.249 | INFO: detected IPv6 address:  | INFO: starting init
 ✗ Joining 2 worker(s) 🚜 6m26s
  invalid argument: the container did not start inside network 'dlx-n736' — the reason is on the line above (exit 1)
  invalid argument: join of worker 'n736-worker2' failed on node 'n736-worker2' (exit 1)
    … dial tcp 10.229.132.236:6443: connect: network is unreachable
```

The quoted init output (`INFO: starting init`) is the kind entrypoint's last line before `exec /sbin/init`. So the init had passed the rootfs setup and run its command.

## What was actually there, 7 minutes later

| | |
|---|---|
| `container ps` | `n736-worker2  Up 7 minutes` |
| record | `status: Running`, `pid: 766858`, `ip: 10.229.26.249`, `network: dlx-n736`, `privileged: true` |
| pid 766858 | `/sbin/init`, alive, parent 766855 = `delonix netns run …/.reexec-4e7b1af9f26c56c2.json` (the 2nd pass, alive) |
| inside the container | only `lo`: no `eth0`, no route |
| `ingress/refs` | one marker (the control-plane); the worker's is gone, `refcount 1` |
| `ipam/*.json` | only the control-plane's lease; `10.229.26.249` is free |
| `n736-worker` | no record at all (its start also failed: «did not start inside network») |

So the two sides disagree. The side that reported `InitExited` (exit 126) ran the failure path and detached the network. The 2nd-pass process (`netns run`) kept an init that was running, and the record says `Running`.

## Why it matters

- **Silent wrong state:** a container reported `Up` with the network it asked for removed.
- **Duplicate IP hazard:** the lease is released while the record and the guest still hold `10.229.26.249`. The next attach on `dlx-n736` can get the same address.
- The error text says «the container is not running». That is false in this case.

## Where to look

`spawn` turns `MountWait::InitExited` into an error for a detached start, after `waitpid(pid)` (`crates/adapters/delonix-linux/src/lib.rs`, `if mounted == MountWait::InitExited && detach`). The same block is on `origin/main`. The 126 came from **some** process exiting, but not from the init that is now running. Open questions:

1. Which process exited 126? In the privileged / console path (kind nodes are `--privileged`, detached, with a log path), is the process waited on the same one whose child holds the «mounted» pipe?
2. Can EOF on the «mounted» pipe arrive while the init is alive? For example, the write end closing in an intermediate process, or the byte written after an `execve` that closed it.
3. On the `--net <custom>` re-exec path, the 1st pass undoes the attach when the 2nd pass reports failure. It never checks whether a process from that start is still alive. Undoing the attach should require proof that nothing from the start survived. A check of the record's pid against its `starttime` would give that.

## Not measured

- Whether this reproduces outside kind mode, or deterministically. Both workers of this run failed; no other attempt was made.

## Summary

`delonix cluster kubeadm` with more than one node finishes «ready», but every node stays `NotReady` (`NetworkPluginNotReady: no CNI network config in /etc/cni/net.d`). The default CNI is installed **only** when the cluster has exactly one node. The code says this is a scope decision (`bins/delonix-runtime-bin/src/cmd/cluster.rs`, the `spec.cni == "default" && … == 1` block; gap #1 of `docs/discovery/kaas-matrix-2026-10-08.md`). There is no issue that tracks closing it.

## Measured (2026-10-11, while validating #753)

Published `delonix-vm-k8s:1.36` plus release v5.0.2, `cluster kubeadm --name k753 --network k753 --control-plane 1 --workers 1`:

```
✓ Bootstrapping control-plane (kubeadm init) 18.2s
✓ Joining 1 worker(s) 6.5s
info cluster "k753" ready
```

Then:

```
k753-cp1   NotReady   control-plane
k753-w1    NotReady   <none>
Ready=False KubeletNotReady: … NetworkPluginNotReady message:no CNI network config in /etc/cni/net.d
coredns-…  0/1  Pending
```

The CNI plugins are on the image (`/opt/cni/bin`). Only the config is missing.

## The manual step that made it work

The step every user hits:

- a `bridge` + `host-local` conflist per node, with a different `/24` of the pod subnet on each (`10.244.0.0/24` on the cp, `10.244.1.0/24` on the worker);
- a static route to the other node's `/24` via its node IP.

Both nodes went `Ready` within seconds. CoreDNS ran. A pod on the cp fetched `http://web.default.svc.cluster.local` from an nginx pod on the worker.

## What a fix needs to decide

- **Per-node pod CIDR.** The controller-manager can allocate `.spec.podCIDR` (`--allocate-node-cidrs`, which kubeadm sets when `--pod-network-cidr` is given). The bridge conflist on each node can use that node's `podCIDR`.
- **Routes between nodes.** These are static, written at join time by the same SSH session that runs `kubeadm join`. Each existing node needs a route to the new node, and the new node needs a route to each existing node. They are not persistent across a node reboot unless written as a systemd-networkd/netplan route. That is a requirement, not an option.
- Or install a real CNI (kindnet is what the kind mode already uses) as a manifest after `kubeadm init`.
- **Honesty in the meantime.** The run printed `cluster "k753" ready` with both nodes `NotReady`. v5.0.2 has no "Waiting for all nodes to be Ready" step; main has one. Whichever path ships, a multi-node cluster must not be reported ready while every node is `NotReady`.

## Not measured

- The behaviour of main's «Waiting for all nodes to be Ready» step against this case (it was v5.0.2 that ran).
- Pod traffic after a node reboot, with routes written as above.
issues.title: cluster kubeadm: a multi-node cluster gets no CNI and stays NotReady

issues.body:
Found while running the battery on 2026-10-11 (plan 68 N30), not fixed.

**Reproduction (measured).** A `build-cache` entry was partially deleted from outside the engine: `rm -rf` on the state root by the invoking user removed what it could and failed with `Permission denied` on files owned by a mapped subuid. A rebuild of the same Delonixfile then hit that cache:

```
FROM alpine:3.19
RUN adduser -D app
USER app
RUN id -u > /home/app/who
USER root
RUN mkdir /srv/own && chown app:app /srv/own
USER app
```

- Root with the partial cache (10 entries): the build succeeds, and running the image gives `--user: user 'app' does not exist in the image (/etc/passwd)`. The entry's `/etc/passwd` was gone, the subuid-owned files stayed, and the cache served the remains as a complete step.
- Fresh root: `who=1000`, owners `app app app root` — correct.

The three battery checks «build: um RUN depois de USER…», «build: um rebuild com cache dá os mesmos donos» and «build: um COPY substitui…» fail in that state and pass on a fresh root.

**Why it matters.** Any interrupted or partial cleanup of the state root (an `rm` that hits subuid files, a crash during a cache write, a full disk) leaves entries the next build trusts. The result is a wrong image that builds without error.

**Expected.** A cache entry is used only when it is known to be complete, for example a marker written last and checked before a hit. Otherwise it is discarded and the step is rebuilt.

Also note: the invoking user cannot remove those entries with `rm` at all (subuid files); the engine's own prune or a mapped removal is the only clean way.
issues.title: build trusts a partially deleted build-cache entry and produces a wrong image

issues.body:
`ContainerService.ListContainers` is declared in the node API contract and not served.
The engine answers `501 / DX-6001`, which is the designed signal for "in the contract,
not implemented yet" — so this is a gap to fill, not a defect to fix.

## Measured

On a staging node running a real workload, against the node API socket:

```
$ curl -sS --unix-socket /run/user/1000/delonix-node.sock -i \
    http://localhost/v1/namespaces/default/containers
HTTP/1.1 501 Not Implemented
content-type: application/problem+json
content-length: 365

{"code":"DX_UNAVAILABLE",
 "detail":"unavailable: ContainerService.ListContainers is in the contract and this engine does not serve it yet",
 "dx":"DX-6001","exit":69,"grpc_status":12,
 "instance":"/v1/namespaces/default/containers",
 "status":501,"title":"the node API does not serve this yet",
 "type":"https://angolardevops.github.io/delonix-runtime/codigos.html#DX-6001"}
```

`grpc_status: 12` is UNIMPLEMENTED, and the problem+json body is the one
`delonix-node-api/src/service.rs:168` formats. The behaviour is deliberate and already
covered by tests (`delonix-node-api/tests/grpc_list_providers.rs:576-642`).

## Where the gap is

- **Declared:** `proto/delonix/node/v1/compute.proto:22` (`service ContainerService`),
  with `rpc ListContainers` at line 32, plus `ListContainersRequest` (:245) and
  `ListContainersResponse` (:280).
- **Served:** nothing. `grep ListContainers crates/interfaces/delonix-node-api/src/`
  returns no handler.
- The node's own `openapi.json` advertises the route, so a client generated from the
  contract compiles, calls, and gets a 501.

## Why it is worth filling

The container is visible through the CLI (`delonix container ls` lists it as `Up`) and
invisible through the API. Anything that consumes the node API rather than shelling out
to the CLI — a console, a monitoring probe, a scheduler, a conformance test — cannot
enumerate containers on a node. It also makes "is this workload actually running?"
answerable only by the component that started it, which is the weaker kind of evidence.

## Note: CRI already has one, and it is a different surface

`crates/interfaces/delonix-cri/src/runtime_svc/lifecycle.rs:2225` implements a
`ListContainers` that returns a `ListContainersResponse` — but that is the **CRI**
service (`delonix-cri/proto/api.proto:70`, the Kubernetes runtime interface), not
`delonix.node.v1.ContainerService`. Worth reading as prior art for the filter semantics
— `lifecycle.rs:4596` documents a filter bug that was fixed there, and the node API
version should not repeat it — but it is not the same RPC and cannot simply be re-exported.

## Done when

- `GET /v1/namespaces/<ns>/containers` returns the containers the node is running, with
  state, and `delonix container ls` and the API agree on the same node.
- The filter in `ListContainersRequest` is honoured, not ignored (see
  `delonix-cri/src/runtime_svc/lifecycle.rs:4596` for how that failed once already).
- A node with zero containers returns an empty list, not a 404 and not a 501.

## Provenance

Surfaced by a staging session whose goal was to prove a real workload runs and responds
on a fresh node: the workload ran, served HTTP from outside the VM, and this was the one
check that could not be closed. Re-measured independently before filing (the output
above). Nothing was explored or modified on the node beyond read-only requests.
issues.title: ContainerService.ListContainers is in the node API contract but not served — 501 / DX-6001

issues.body:
## Context

ADR-0043 (`docs/adr/0043-error-code-dictionary.md`) gives every concrete failure a `DX-CDNN` number. The good end-state is already visible in the wild — a mid-pull registry failure (2026-11-17) printed:

```
error[DX-9401] registry error: layer sha256:bbe6…: gave up after 5 attempts with 1015788 of 8714240 bytes — last error: … tcp connect error: Connection refused (os error 111)
```

Code, origin, cause chain, quantified context. That is the bar.

But the ADR's own measurement (2026-09-17, origin/main) found **~460 call sites in the adapters still building the shared error with a free-text message** (246 `Invalid`, 143 `Runtime`), and 50–90 sites matching directly on shared-error variants. Nothing measures this today, so coverage can regress silently.

## Ask (slice 1 of the campaign — measurement, not fixes)

1. A script (`scripts/`-style, like `lang_ratchet.py`) that counts, per crate: error sites with a DX number vs free-text `Invalid`/`Runtime` construction, with a bilateral baseline so the count can neither rise nor silently drop.
2. A report naming the top user-facing offenders — messages that state neither origin, cause, nor remedy — each with file+symbol anchors, ordered by user impact (CLI-facing first).
3. The gate wired into CI like the other ratchets.

Rewriting the messages themselves is explicitly out of scope here; each domain gets its own follow-up session fed by the report.
issues.title: errors: measure DX-CDNN dictionary coverage and ratchet it (semantic error tracker, slice 1)

issues.body:
## Observed (rootless host, 2026-11-17)

```
$ delonix container run --rm httpd
AH00558: httpd: Could not reliably determine the server's fully qualified domain name …
(13)Permission denied: AH00072: make_sock: could not bind to address [::]:80
(13)Permission denied: AH00072: make_sock: could not bind to address 0.0.0.0:80
no listening sockets available, shutting down
```

The user gets the workload's own cryptic error, with no hint that the cause is delonix sharing the HOST netns.

## Diagnosis

- Default is `--net host` (`bins/delonix/src/cmd/container.rs`, arg `net`, `default_value = "host"`): rootless, the container shares the host netns, where an unprivileged process cannot bind <1024 (`ip_unprivileged_port_start=1024`, no `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`).
- The own-netns path already works: `run -d -p 8080:80 httpd` + `curl 127.0.0.1:8080` → **200** (measured 2026-11-17), even with the netns sysctl still at 1024 — the mapped-root userns caps allow the bind.
- The CRI path already solves this for pods: `pod_netns_sysctls` (`crates/interfaces/delonix-cri/src/runtime_svc/lifecycle.rs`) writes `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=0` (containerd 2.x defaults; CoreDNS uid 65532 died without it, measured 2026-09-15).
- The HOST side of this is already semantic: `can_bind_host_port` + the "binding port p on the host needs privilege … publish on a higher port instead" hint. The inside is what lacks the equivalent.

## Design decision — deliberately open

(a) **Preflight**: rootless + `--net host` + image EXPOSEs a port <1024 → warn or refuse with a DX error naming cause and remedy (`-p 8080:80` or `--net <network>`); or
(b) **Change the rootless default to an own netns** (parity with rootless Docker/Podman, whose default is bridge/own-netns — why `httpd` just works there). More invasive; touches networks, DNS and the published tables.

Either way: never again the bare AH00072.
issues.title: rootless: container run with default --net host fails to bind ports <1024 with the workload's own cryptic error

## Phase 1 — Windows/WSL2 launcher (ADR-0036)

[ADR-0036](docs/adr/0036-macos-windows-support.md) is now **Accepted** and Phase 1
(Windows/WSL2) is greenlit. macOS/Windows support is a **guest-VM launcher**, not a
port of the engine — the host-native binary drives a Linux guest that runs the
unmodified engine. This issue tracks the Windows half, which rides on WSL2 (a real
Linux kernel Microsoft already ships), so it needs **no new hypervisor code**.

### Scope (Phase 1)
- New crate `delonix-machine`, compiled **only** for `target_os = "windows"` (and later
  `"macos"`) via `[target.'cfg(...)'.dependencies]`. **Zero** new deps and **zero** new
  `#[cfg]` branches on any Linux crate — a Linux build stays byte-for-byte unaffected.
- A `Machine` variant on the CLI `Cmd` enum, compiled only on those targets.
- A thin Rust wrapper shelling out to `wsl.exe`:
  - `init [--memory --cpus]` → `wsl --import <distro> <dir> <rootfs>` from the published
    `delonix-vm-base` image (tar-packaged for `wsl --import`; a packaging step, not an
    image rebuild).
  - `start` / `stop` / `rm` / `list`
  - `ssh` → interactive shell in the guest
  - `exec -- <any delonix command>` → `wsl -d <distro> -- delonix ...`

### First design question (resolve before code)
The CLI **already** uses `delonix machine` for IaC-stack drift ("what the MACHINE
changed since the last apply"). The launcher **cannot** silently reuse that verb. Pick a
non-colliding surface (e.g. `delonix wsl …` on Windows, or a different noun) and record
the decision here.

### CI (the honest bar)
Add a `windows-latest` job that (a) compiles the crate and (b) round-trips
`wsl --import` + `exec` against a real (GitHub-hosted) WSL2. A compiled-but-never-run
binary is not "supported".

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Naming conflict resolved and documented.
- [ ] `delonix-machine` compiles on `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`; Linux build unchanged (no new deps/`#[cfg]` on Linux crates).
- [ ] `init`/`exec` round-trip proven on a `windows-latest` CI job against real WSL2.
- [ ] Docs: a "run Delonix on Windows" quickstart.

### Out of scope (this issue)
- Phase 2 (macOS/Virtualization.framework) — gated on a GO/NO-GO spike on real Mac hardware.
- A GUI; host↔guest networking parity with the Linux SDN; `arm64` guest images (ADR-0018, separate gap).

Refs: ADR-0036 (Accepted 2026-11-19).
issues.title: macOS/Windows Phase 1: Windows/WSL2 launcher (ADR-0036)
